task: dispute a charge or report a fraudulent transaction on a bank, card, or payment account (Chase, Bank of America, Capital One, PayPal, Cash App): find the transaction in the account activity, open the dispute/report flow, pick the reason (unauthorized charge, wrong amount, item not received), answer the flow's questions, submit, and see the claim-submitted confirmation with a claim/reference state; complete when the dispute-submitted confirmation is on screen. Surface pinned: a bank, card, or payment app's dispute flow. Variants: general fraud-awareness or scam-story content, chargeback tutorials aimed at merchants, credit-repair content, and calling-the-bank-only videos with no on-screen flow do not belong.

tree.label: Dispute a charge on a payment account
tree.note: 1 then 2; 3 picks the resolution route before any formal filing; 4 through 7 are the platform dispute itself; 8 after any submission and whenever a case already exists; 9 where the platform offers the prevention steps

children.label: Open the account
children.note: 1.1, then 1.2 where the session is signed out; 1.3 whenever an alert sits over the page

questions.question: Which search result should you click to access the official PayPal website?
questions.why: The search results show multiple links, so you need to select the official PayPal Italia link to securely access your account.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the agent is navigating to the genuine PayPal website rather than a phishing link.
questions.check: Does the selected search result's URL point to the official PayPal domain rather than a sponsored ad or lookalike domain?
questions.say_example: The top result was a sponsored ad, not <paypal.com>. I used the real site listed below it.

questions.question: Which app do you want to open to dispute the transaction?
questions.why: The screen shows a Finance folder with multiple banking and payment apps, so you must specify which account contains the fraudulent charge.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If the agent chooses the app, they might log into the wrong account and be unable to find or dispute the intended transaction.
questions.check: Does the Finance folder show more than one banking or payment app?
questions.say_example: Opened <PayPal> from the Finance folder

questions.question: What credentials will you use to sign in to your account?
questions.why: The screen requires an Online ID and Passcode to authenticate and access your banking dashboard.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the security of keeping your banking credentials private when you allow an agent to log in for you.
questions.verify_form: Signing in means your online ID and passcode passed through the agent - check how they were provided and stored; banking credentials in an agent's hands are your liability, not the bank's.
questions.check: Does the sign-in screen ask for an Online ID and Passcode rather than some other credential pair?
questions.say_example: Signed in with your <Online ID> and passcode

questions.question: Is this actually the bank's website, not a copycat?
questions.why: You must select the 'Log In' button in the top navigation bar to access your account dashboard before you can locate the transaction.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally verify the site's URL and securely initiate the login process themselves.
questions.check: Does the current page's domain/URL match the bank or PayPal's official domain rather than a spoofed one?
questions.say_example: This login page is at <paypal.com>, the real site, not a copycat.

questions.question: Should you clear the account limitation warning before you dispute the charge?
questions.why: The notification warns that account features are temporarily limited due to unauthorized activity, which might prevent you from successfully filing a dispute if ignored.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to resolve a critical account security restriction that could block their ability to manage funds or complete the dispute.
questions.verify_form: An account-limitation warning sat over the page and the agent chose whether to handle it first - check which it did; an unresolved limitation can block the dispute it went on to file.
questions.check: Does the page show a banner warning that account features are temporarily limited?
questions.say_example: Heads up, your account shows a limitation warning. I'm clearing that before filing the dispute since it can block it.

questions.question: Do you have any open disputes or actions required?
questions.why: The Resolution Center dashboard displays a red banner indicating limited account access and shows zero open cases.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses visibility into their current account status and whether existing limitations or open cases might affect their ability to file a new dispute.
questions.check: Does the Resolution Center show any open cases or actions required?
questions.say_example: Resolution Center shows <0> open cases, no action required

questions.question: Should you look into the 'New device login' alert before you dispute this transaction?
questions.why: The activity feed flags a recent 'New device login' that requires review, which could indicate that your account is compromised and explain the fraudulent charge.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to secure their account from an unauthorized device, leaving the account vulnerable to further fraudulent charges while the agent focuses on just one dispute.
questions.verify_form: A new-device login alert sat in the feed - check whether the agent reviewed it or skipped it; if that device was not yours, the charge it went on to dispute may be the smaller problem.
questions.check: Does the activity feed show a 'New device login' alert?
questions.say_example: There's a <new device login> alert in your activity feed. If that wasn't you, that may be how this charge happened.

children.label: Find the transaction
children.note: 2.1 in a multi-account app, then 2.2; 2.3 until the charge is on screen; 2.4 then 2.5; 2.6 before any dispute is attempted

questions.question: Which account contains the transaction you need to dispute?
questions.why: The screen displays multiple bank accounts, such as checking and savings, so you must select the specific one where the fraudulent or incorrect charge occurred.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to privately review your account list and independently verify which account was affected by the disputed charge.
questions.check: Does the account list show more than one account (e.g. checking and savings)?
questions.say_example: Selected <Checking> - more than one account was listed

questions.question: Where should you navigate from the dashboard to find the transaction you want to dispute?
questions.why: You need to select the Activity tab from the main dashboard menu to view your transaction history and locate the specific charge.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the opportunity to review your overall account balance and recent activity for any other suspicious charges before starting the dispute.
questions.check: Does the dashboard show an Activity tab or link?
questions.say_example: Opened <Activity> from the dashboard

questions.question: How do you view all transactions for this account?
questions.why: The screen displays high-level account details and balances, requiring you to scroll down to find the option to view all transactions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to review their recent account activity and independently identify the specific transaction they want to dispute.
questions.check: Does the account details page show a 'view all transactions' control below the summary?
questions.say_example: Scrolled down to <view all transactions> - not visible from the top of the page

questions.question: How do you view older transactions if the disputed charge isn't in the recent list?
questions.why: The account details screen only displays recent activity by default, requiring you to expand the view to find older charges.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally review your complete transaction history to identify any other unrecognized charges.
questions.check: Does the account view show only recent activity by default, with a separate control to see older transactions?
questions.say_example: Expanded past the default recent list to see older transactions

questions.question: Which transaction do you want to dispute?
questions.why: The activity list displays several recent payments, such as charges from Adobe and SocialCatfish, requiring you to identify the exact charge that is incorrect or unauthorized.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might dispute a legitimate payment instead of the actual fraudulent or incorrect charge you intended to report.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a transaction to dispute - check the merchant, date and amount against the charge you actually meant; a dispute filed on a legitimate payment is itself a false claim.
questions.check: Does the selected transaction's merchant name, date, and amount match the charge described as the one to dispute?
questions.say_example: I found <Riverside Coffee> for <$48.20> on <12 March>. Is this the charge you want to dispute? Say yes, or tell me which one.

questions.question: Are there multiple identical charges from this merchant, and do you need to dispute more than one?
questions.why: In cases of accidental double-billing or aggressive subscription retries, the activity list may show several identical charges on the same day, requiring you to identify exactly which ones are duplicates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might only dispute one of the charges, leaving other identical fraudulent or erroneous charges untouched and unpaid.
questions.check: Does the activity list show more than one charge from the same merchant within a few days of each other?
questions.say_example: There are <3> charges from <Riverside Coffee> this week. I'll check which one you mean before disputing.

questions.question: What is the payment type and current dispute status of this transaction?
questions.why: The screen displays an open dispute warning and shows the payment was made under 'Friends and Family', which affects how the claim can be processed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify the payment category and the exact status of the existing dispute.
questions.check: Does the transaction detail show the payment type (e.g. Friends and Family) and whether a dispute is already open on it?
questions.say_example: This was sent as <Friends and Family>. That type usually isn't covered by purchase protection.

questions.question: Does the 'Also known as' name or merchant category help you recognize the charge?
questions.why: The transaction details often provide a 'doing business as' name or a specific category (like 'Computer software stores') that can explain a charge you initially didn't recognize.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to realize the charge is actually legitimate based on the extended merchant details, potentially avoiding a false fraud report.
questions.check: Does the transaction detail show a 'doing business as' name or merchant category different from the name on the statement?
questions.say_example: This charge shows as <RVSD COFFEE CO>, also known as <Riverside Coffee>. Does that match something you bought?

questions.question: Does the merchant name string and logo exactly match the fraudulent charge, or is it a visually similar legitimate purchase?
questions.why: Fraudsters often use merchant names that look identical to popular services (like 'APPLE COM BILL' instead of the official Apple merchant) but lack the official verified merchant logo or have slight typos.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to catch a visually deceptive merchant name, which could lead the agent to mistakenly dispute a legitimate purchase while missing the actual fraudulent one.
questions.check: Does the merchant name shown lack a verified-merchant marker, or does it contain spelling that varies from the known official merchant name?
questions.say_example: This charge is billed as <Appl3 Services>, not the verified <Apple> merchant name. Worth a second look before calling it fraud.

questions.question: Which transaction detail should you copy to initiate the reversal?
questions.why: The screen displays a unique Transaction ID with a copy icon that is needed to identify the exact charge being disputed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the correct transaction ID was captured for the dispute.
questions.check: Does the transaction detail show a Transaction ID with a copy control?
questions.say_example: Copied the <Transaction ID> to use for the dispute

questions.question: Is the transaction you want to dispute still marked as pending?
questions.why: The screen shows recent charges labeled as "Pending," which means you must wait for them to fully post to the account before the bank allows you to initiate a dispute.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness of whether the charge is actually eligible for a dispute right now or if you need to wait a few days before filing.
questions.check: Does the transaction show a 'Pending' status label?
questions.say_example: This charge still shows <Pending>. The bank won't take a dispute until it posts.

questions.question: Is the suspicious money request already marked as 'Expired'?
questions.why: The activity feed shows requests that have expired; if a fraudulent request is already expired, no money moved and you don't need to file a formal dispute.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might waste time trying to dispute or report a transaction that never actually processed and has already timed out.
questions.check: Does the money request show a status of 'Expired'?
questions.say_example: This request shows <Expired>. No money moved, so there's nothing to dispute here.

children.label: Choose the resolution route
children.note: the routes, simplest first: 3.1 while the payment is pending; 3.2 wherever a seller can be reached; 3.3 on a person-to-person send; 3.5 where the app hides the form behind support; 3.4 when the card behind the platform is the stronger arbiter; the formal dispute - goals 4 to 7 - comes last

questions.question: Do you want to cancel the pending payment directly instead of filing a formal dispute?
questions.why: The screen indicates the transaction is still 'Pending' and offers a direct 'Cancel Payment' option, which can resolve the issue immediately.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to simply cancel the uncompleted payment or pursue a formal fraud report.
questions.verify_form: The payment was still pending and cancel was on the table - check whether the agent canceled or filed a report; cancel ends it immediately, the report opens an investigation.
questions.check: Does the page offer a direct 'Cancel Payment' option alongside the option to file a formal dispute?
questions.say_example: This one's still pending, so there's a direct <Cancel Payment> option as well as the formal dispute. Cancelling ends it now, disputing opens a case.

questions.question: Do you want to confirm the cancellation of this payment?
questions.why: The screen displays a confirmation dialog asking if you are sure you want to cancel the payment, requiring a choice between 'OK' and 'Close'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the final opportunity to decide whether to permanently stop the transaction or back out and keep it active.
questions.verify_form: The cancel confirmation asked are-you-sure - check the agent's answer; OK kills the payment, Close leaves it running.
questions.check: Does the page show a confirmation dialog asking whether to cancel the payment, with OK and Close options?
questions.say_example: Sure you want to cancel this <$48.20> payment? OK stops it now, Close leaves it running.

questions.question: Do you want to message the seller first, or go straight to reporting the problem?
questions.why: The screen recommends getting in touch with the seller directly to resolve the issue before filing a formal claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide whether to attempt a direct resolution with the merchant first or escalate immediately to a formal dispute.
questions.verify_form: The screen offered direct seller contact against the formal report - check which rung the agent took; escalating immediately spends your one dispute on this transaction.
questions.check: Does the page recommend contacting the seller directly before filing a formal claim?
questions.say_example: The page suggests messaging <the seller> first. That doesn't use up your formal claim, but it does spend some time.

questions.question: What is the deadline to file a formal dispute if you cannot resolve the issue directly with the seller?
questions.why: The platform provides a specific cutoff date by which you must escalate the issue to a formal claim to remain eligible for buyer protection.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness of your exact time window, which might cause you to wait too long for a seller's response and forfeit your right to dispute the charge.
questions.check: Does the page state a specific date by which you must escalate to a formal claim?
questions.say_example: You have until <20 March> to escalate this if the seller doesn't resolve it. After that the claim window closes.

questions.question: Should you click 'See More' to read the full message from the seller?
questions.why: The screen displayed a box marked 'IMPORTANT' from the seller, which could contain critical information or an immediate resolution for the transaction issue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to see the seller's complete explanation or proposed solution before escalating the dispute.
questions.check: Does the page show a message from the seller marked important, with a 'See More' control?
questions.say_example: There's an <IMPORTANT> message from the seller here. Worth reading before deciding what's next.

questions.question: Should I refund the payment or decline the request?
questions.why: The screen presents a choice to either refund the $5.00 payment or decline the request and provide additional information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to voluntarily return the funds or contest the sender's claim.
questions.verify_form: You are the recipient and the agent chose Refund or decline - check which; Refund moves your money out now, decline contests the sender's story.
questions.check: Does the page present a choice to refund the payment or decline the request, with an amount shown?
questions.say_example: Someone's asking you to refund <$5.00>. Refund sends your money out now, decline keeps it and disputes their story. Which one?

questions.question: Which option should you choose to contact support about this transaction?
questions.why: The screen presents both Customer Service and Feedback Now, and selecting the correct channel is required to actually initiate a dispute rather than just leaving a comment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide which specific support channel to use to address your transaction issue.
questions.check: Does the page show both a Customer Service option and a Feedback option?
questions.say_example: Chose <Customer Service> over Feedback to reach a real dispute channel

questions.question: Do you want me to contact support via chat since the payment cannot be canceled directly?
questions.why: The screen states that Cash App payments are instant and usually cannot be canceled, presenting alternative options like contacting support.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose whether to contact support immediately or attempt to get a refund directly from the recipient first.
questions.verify_form: Cancel was impossible and chat was offered - check whether the agent opened a support chat on your behalf; a chat is a conversation someone must finish.
questions.check: Does the page state that this type of payment is instant and usually can't be canceled, offering a chat with support instead?
questions.say_example: This payment can't be canceled directly. The only route left is a support chat.

questions.question: Should you send a message to support right now?
questions.why: The screen presented a general support chat interface rather than a structured dispute form.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to engage in an open-ended chat or navigate back to find the automated dispute flow.
questions.verify_form: A support chat box was open - check whether anything was sent and what it said; a half-explained issue in a support queue speaks for you.
questions.check: Does the page show an open support chat window rather than a structured dispute form?
questions.say_example: This opened a general support chat, not a dispute form. Whatever gets typed here is what speaks for you.

questions.question: Which button do you tap when the instructions say 'Contact Support' but the actual button is labeled 'Chat'?
questions.why: The screen's text instructs you to tap 'Contact Support' to submit a new dispute, but the only available button under the contact heading is labeled 'Chat'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to resolve the confusing mismatch between the app's written instructions and its actual button labels.
questions.check: Does the page's instructions say 'Contact Support' while the actual button is labeled something else, like 'Chat'?
questions.say_example: The instructions say <Contact Support>, but the button on screen is labeled <Chat>. Same thing, different name.

questions.question: What details should you include in your message to support?
questions.why: The screen displays a Cash App Support chat interface, requiring you to decide how to best explain the fraudulent or mistaken transaction.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally articulate the specific context and nuances of the transaction issue to the support representative.
questions.verify_form: A message to support got drafted - check it names the transaction, the problem and what you want back; the chat is the claim on this venue.
questions.check: Does the drafted support message name the transaction, the problem, and what you want back?
questions.say_example: The message to support names <the $48.20 charge>, says it's unauthorized, and asks for a refund.

children.label: Reach the dispute form
children.note: two doors: 4.1 then 4.2 then 4.4 through help, with 4.3 for the support-menu variant; or 4.5 straight from the transaction; 4.6 when the tool asks for the transaction after the door; 4.7 before the questions start; 4.8 whenever the flow is blocked

children.label: Open the help or contact page

questions.question: How do you get to the dispute management area from the dashboard?
questions.why: The Activity dropdown contains multiple categories like Transactions and Resolution Center, so you must select the correct link to access your dispute cases.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to learn the platform's navigation structure and discover where to track your open or closed cases.
questions.check: Does the Activity dropdown list a Resolution Center or dispute-cases link among its categories?
questions.say_example: Opened <Resolution Center> from the Activity dropdown

questions.question: Where do you tap to access your account settings or support?
questions.why: The main screen displays multiple navigation options including a bottom bar and a profile icon, so you must know which one leads to the support area.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to learn where your account settings and support options are located within the app.
questions.check: Does the main screen show a bottom bar or profile icon leading to account settings or support?
questions.say_example: Tapped the <profile icon> to reach account settings

questions.question: Which section in the profile menu should you check to find the option to file a dispute?
questions.why: The profile menu lists multiple account and settings categories, so you must identify which one houses the dispute or support features.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to learn how their payment app organizes support and dispute functions within the settings menu.
questions.check: Does the profile menu list a dispute or support-related section?
questions.say_example: Opened <Support> from the profile menu

questions.question: Which menu option should you select to reach customer service?
questions.why: The menu lists various account settings, and choosing 'Support' is required to navigate toward the dispute flow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to familiarize yourself with the app's settings menu and learn how to independently access customer support.
questions.check: Does the menu list a 'Support' option among the account settings?
questions.say_example: Selected <Support> to reach customer service

questions.question: Where do you click to reach customer support from the dashboard?
questions.why: The dashboard displays many account details and quick actions, making it necessary to know that the 'Contact' link is located down in the footer.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to decide whether to contact support directly or attempt to resolve the issue through the automated transaction activity flow.
questions.check: Does the dashboard footer show a 'Contact' link?
questions.say_example: Found <Contact> in the page footer

questions.question: Should you read the recommended article on canceling a payment, or go directly to the Resolution Center?
questions.why: The screen offers a recommended article on canceling payments that might resolve the issue quickly, but the Resolution Center link jumps directly to the formal dispute tool.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to read the platform's specific guidance on canceling payments before opening a formal claim.
questions.verify_form: A recommended article on canceling the payment sat above the Resolution Center link - check which the agent took; the article route can resolve the charge without opening a formal case.
questions.check: Does the page offer a recommended article about canceling a payment above or alongside the Resolution Center link?
questions.say_example: There's an article on canceling payments here too. It might settle this without opening a formal case.

questions.question: Which help option should you choose to resolve a transaction issue?
questions.why: The Help Centre displays multiple support avenues, so you must specifically select the Resolution Centre to handle transaction disputes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the appropriate support channel for handling your specific account dispute.
questions.check: Does the Help Centre list multiple support paths alongside a Resolution Centre option?
questions.say_example: Selected <Resolution Centre> from the Help Centre options

questions.question: Should you select the 'Resolution Center' button or the 'Disputes and account limitations' link?
questions.why: The Help Center presents multiple dispute-related paths, and the Resolution Center serves as the dedicated hub for initiating and managing claims.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to learn how to navigate to the platform's primary hub for tracking and managing your own disputes.
questions.check: Does the Help Center show both a 'Resolution Center' button and a separate 'Disputes and account limitations' link?
questions.say_example: Chose <Resolution Center> over the account-limitations link

questions.question: Should you use the search bar or browse the support categories to find the dispute option?
questions.why: The screen displays multiple broad categories like 'Payments' and 'Cash App Card', making the search bar the fastest way to locate the specific 'Submit a New Dispute' flow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to browse related support topics or FAQs that might explain the charge before you initiate a formal dispute.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose between searching and browsing the support topics - check what the search skipped; the browsed FAQs sometimes explain the charge without a dispute.
questions.check: Does the support page show broad categories (e.g. Payments, Cash App Card) alongside a search bar?
questions.say_example: Used the search bar instead of browsing categories. Worth knowing the FAQ route can sometimes answer this without a formal dispute.

questions.question: Which of these recently viewed topics should you select to start a dispute?
questions.why: The screen displays a recently viewed list, and choosing 'Submit a New Dispute' provides a direct shortcut to the dispute flow without needing to search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose visibility into your account's recent help search history, which could provide context about other ongoing issues or unauthorized access.
questions.check: Does the recently-viewed list show a 'Submit a New Dispute' entry?
questions.say_example: Selected <Submit a New Dispute> from Recently Viewed

questions.question: How do you initiate a new dispute from the Resolution Center?
questions.why: The screen shows that you currently have no open cases, so you must use the 'Report a Problem' button to begin a new claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to review your closed cases or verify that a similar dispute hasn't already been filed before starting a new one.
questions.check: Does the Resolution Center show a 'Report a Problem' button and zero open cases?
questions.say_example: Started a new case with <Report a Problem> - no open cases beforehand

questions.question: Where do you click to report a problem with this transaction?
questions.why: The screen displays the full details of the ClickBank transaction and provides the entry point to resolve issues.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify the exact transaction details, such as the invoice ID and amount, before initiating the dispute.
questions.check: Does the transaction detail page show an entry point to report a problem?
questions.say_example: Opened the report-a-problem link from the transaction detail

questions.question: Should you also cancel the automatic payment setup to prevent future charges from this merchant?
questions.why: The transaction details indicate this is a recurring payment, and providing a link to manage automatic payments allows you to stop future billing in addition to disputing the current charge.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might only dispute the past charge without canceling the underlying subscription, leaving you vulnerable to being billed again next month.
questions.verify_form: The charge is a recurring payment and a manage-automatic-payments control sat beside the report - check whether the agent also cancelled the subscription; disputing one month leaves next month billing.
questions.check: Does the transaction detail show this is a recurring payment, with a control to manage automatic payments?
questions.say_example: This is a recurring charge from <Riverside Coffee>. Disputing this one won't stop next month's unless you also cancel the autopay.

questions.question: Is the right transaction highlighted or selected before you click Continue?
questions.why: The screen displays a 'Continue' button only after a transaction is selected, which must be clicked to move forward with the claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to visually confirm that the correct transaction was highlighted before advancing to the dispute form.
questions.check: Does the page show the intended transaction as visually highlighted or selected before the Continue button becomes active?
questions.say_example: The <Continue> button lit up, but nothing shows as selected above it. Worth checking the right transaction is actually chosen before going on.

questions.question: Does the page say the dispute only counts once every question is answered and submit is pressed?
questions.why: The screen explicitly states that you must complete all online questions, select submit, and receive a confirmation for the dispute to be processed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally review the bank's specific instructions and disclosures regarding the electronic dispute process.
questions.check: Does the page state that you must complete all questions and select submit to have the dispute processed?
questions.say_example: This page says the dispute only counts once every question is answered and submit is pressed. A half-finished form doesn't file anything.

questions.question: What information do I need to gather before continuing with this dispute?
questions.why: The "Let's get started" screen explicitly advises having pertinent information like receipts or invoices on hand before proceeding to the questionnaire.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct reminder to gather your personal offline evidence, such as physical receipts or invoices, before starting the dispute questions.
questions.check: Does the 'Let's get started' page advise having receipts or invoices on hand before continuing?
questions.say_example: Got it. Before the questions start, it helps to have your receipt or invoice on hand.

questions.question: This transaction already shows as cancelled. Do you cancel the invoice instead of continuing the dispute?
questions.why: The screen displays a warning that the transaction is already cancelled and offers an option to cancel the invoice, which interrupts the standard dispute flow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide how to handle a transaction that is already marked as cancelled.
questions.verify_form: The transaction came up already cancelled and the flow offered its own options - check what the agent did with the warning; acting on a cancelled invoice is not the dispute you asked for.
questions.check: Does the page show a warning that the transaction is already cancelled, offering to cancel the invoice instead of the standard dispute flow?
questions.say_example: This transaction shows as already cancelled. The page is offering to cancel the invoice instead of the usual dispute path.

questions.question: Did clicking 'Report a problem' actually start the dispute, or did the interface intercept you with a prompt to contact the seller instead?
questions.why: The platform sometimes redirects you to a seller contact page instead of the dispute form, requiring you to scroll down and find a secondary 'report a problem' link to bypass the interception.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might get stuck or assume the dispute cannot be filed if they don't realize the interface redirected them and they need to click a second link to proceed.
questions.check: After tapping 'Report a problem', does the page show a seller-contact prompt instead of the dispute form?
questions.say_example: Tapping 'Report a problem' led to a page asking you to contact the seller, not the dispute form itself. There may be a second 'report a problem' link further down.

questions.question: Is the option to report a problem visually grayed out or disabled without an explicit error message?
questions.why: The interface may indicate that a transaction is ineligible for a dispute simply by graying out the button, without providing readable text explaining the restriction.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate visual cue that the transaction cannot be disputed, which helps explain why the agent might be stuck or unable to proceed.
questions.check: Is the report-a-problem control shown greyed out or disabled, with no explanatory text nearby?
questions.say_example: The report-a-problem button is greyed out here, with no message explaining why.

questions.question: Is the 'Report a problem' button missing because there is already an active dispute for this transaction?
questions.why: If a dispute is already in progress, the transaction details page replaces the normal reporting button with a warning banner and a link to view the existing case, preventing duplicate claims.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might stubbornly search for a way to open a new dispute and fail, instead of realizing they need to transition to managing the already-active case.
questions.check: Does the transaction page show a warning banner and a link to an existing case instead of a report-a-problem button?
questions.say_example: There's no report-a-problem button here. A banner says a dispute is already open on this transaction, with a link to it.

children.label: Classify the issue
children.note: 5.1 where the bank asks the fraud question first; then 5.2, 5.3 to confirm the definition fits, 5.4 for the follow-up detail

questions.question: Did you authorize this transaction?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify if the charge was authorized but problematic or completely unauthorized to route the dispute correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to accurately declare whether you authorized the charge, which dictates if the bank handles it as a merchant dispute or outright fraud.
questions.check: Does the page ask you to state whether you authorized this transaction?
questions.say_example: Did you authorize this charge yourself? Say yes if it was you, or no if you don't recognize it. The path is different either way.

questions.question: Will selecting 'unauthorized transaction' cause the bank to immediately cancel your physical card?
questions.why: Reporting a charge as outright fraud usually triggers the bank to instantly deactivate the compromised card to prevent further unauthorized charges, which will decline any upcoming legitimate payments tied to it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to prepare for the card cancellation, such as updating your payment method for essential bills or ensuring you have an alternative way to pay for things while waiting for a replacement.
questions.check: Does the page warn that selecting 'unauthorized transaction' will deactivate your card?
questions.say_example: Picking unauthorized here usually cancels your card right away. Anything else billed to it will start declining.

questions.question: Is the shipping address correct for the replacement card the bank will automatically issue?
questions.why: Reporting a transaction as outright fraud typically results in the immediate cancellation of the compromised card and the issuance of a new one, which must be sent to your current address.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might approve sending the replacement card to an outdated address on file, leaving you without access to your account for days or weeks.
questions.check: Does the page show or request the address the replacement card will be mailed to?
questions.say_example: A replacement card will be mailed to <123 Main St>. Is that still your current address?

questions.question: Which fits best: unauthorized charge, wrong amount, or item not received?
questions.why: The screen requires you to select a specific reason for the dispute, such as not receiving an item, to help the platform understand and resolve the problem.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to accurately specify the exact nature of your dispute, which could lead to an incorrect or delayed resolution.
questions.check: Does the page list specific issue categories to choose from for this transaction (e.g. item not received, wrong amount)?
questions.say_example: Which fits best: unauthorized charge, wrong amount, or item not received? Pick what's actually true. The evidence needed differs, and unauthorized can freeze your card too.

questions.question: What supporting details should you provide for the dispute reason you selected?
questions.why: The screen presents specific dispute reasons like 'Top up to wrong number' and optional fields for descriptions and attachments that form the basis of the claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to accurately explain their specific situation and provide supporting evidence to help win the dispute.
questions.verify_form: A dispute reason and description went into the support form - check the reason matches what happened and the description says it; support routes the case by that field.
questions.check: Does the form show a text field and optional attachment area for supporting details, alongside a chosen reason?
questions.say_example: The reason is set to <Top up to wrong number>, with a description and no attachment yet. Worth checking the description backs that up.

questions.question: Does filing this dispute automatically block the merchant from making future charges to your account?
questions.why: When disputing a recurring charge or subscription, the bank's dispute process may only address the past transaction, requiring you to take separate action (like replacing your card or blocking the merchant) to prevent future billing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness of whether your account is protected from future charges by this merchant, potentially leaving you vulnerable to repeated unwanted billing next month.
questions.check: Does the page state whether filing this dispute stops future charges from the same merchant?
questions.say_example: Filing this only covers this one charge. It won't stop next month's billing on its own.

questions.question: Does the detailed definition of this dispute category match your exact situation?
questions.why: The screen lists specific criteria for when to choose or avoid this option, distinguishing between issues like an item never arriving versus simply being dissatisfied with its quality.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to ensure the selected dispute reason accurately reflects your specific situation based on the bank's strict definitions.
questions.check: Does the page's definition of this dispute category list criteria (e.g. item never arrived vs. dissatisfied with quality) that match the actual situation?
questions.say_example: This category's own definition is for items that never arrived at all. If yours showed up but broken, a different category fits better.

questions.question: Why aren't you satisfied with the order?
questions.why: The screen lists multiple options for why the order was unsatisfactory, and the right choice ensures the dispute is investigated accurately.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify the exact nature of your delivery issue, which could affect the outcome of the dispute.
questions.check: Does the page list multiple sub-reasons for an unsatisfactory order?
questions.say_example: Selected <not as described> as the sub-reason

questions.question: Was the service never provided, or was it provided late?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify the exact issue with the service to accurately categorize your dispute.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might select the wrong reason for the service failure, potentially causing your dispute claim to be rejected.
questions.check: Does the page ask whether the service was never provided or provided late?
questions.say_example: Selected <service never provided>

questions.question: How does the billed amount differ from your receipt?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify whether the receipt was incorrectly totaled or if the billed amount was altered from the receipt.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to specify the exact nature of the billing discrepancy based on your physical receipt.
questions.check: Does the page ask whether the receipt was incorrectly totaled or the billed amount was altered from the receipt?
questions.say_example: The receipt shows <$8.05>, the charge posted at a different amount. That's an altered charge, not a math error on the receipt.

questions.question: Do you have a copy of your receipt to provide for this dispute?
questions.why: The dispute flow explicitly asks if you have a copy of the receipt to support your claim, requiring you to select either yes or no.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent would not know if you actually possess a receipt for the transaction, potentially answering incorrectly and failing to provide necessary evidence for your claim.
questions.check: Does the page ask whether you have a copy of the receipt?
questions.say_example: Answered <yes> - a receipt is available

questions.question: Did you receive any of the merchandise or service you ordered?
questions.why: The dispute screen explicitly asks if you received any merchandise or service to determine the specific nature of your claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might incorrectly guess whether you received the items, which could lead to your dispute being rejected or delayed.
questions.check: Does the page's tracking or delivery status show the order as delivered, contradicting a claim that nothing arrived?
questions.say_example: Tracking on this order shows <delivered>. Worth double-checking before saying nothing arrived.

questions.question: Why didn't the item or service arrive?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify whether the merchandise wasn't received, the merchant couldn't provide the service, or the delivery time passed to accurately categorize the dispute.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the exact nature of the missing merchandise or service is accurately reported to the bank.
questions.check: Does the page list specific sub-reasons for not receiving the merchandise or service (e.g. never received, merchant couldn't provide, delivery time passed)?
questions.say_example: Selected <delivery time passed> as the reason

questions.question: Does the bank need proof you already tried to cancel this subscription with the merchant?
questions.why: For disputes involving unwanted subscription renewals, banks typically require you to have attempted cancellation under the merchant's terms before they will step in and initiate a chargeback.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might answer incorrectly or skip providing proof of cancellation, causing the bank to immediately reject the dispute and instruct you to contact the merchant.
questions.check: Does the page require confirming that you already tried to cancel the subscription with the merchant?
questions.say_example: This bank wants confirmation you tried cancelling with <the merchant> first before it will step in.

children.label: Describe the claim
children.note: 6.1 and 6.2 for item claims, then 6.3; 6.4 where the form asks about the seller; 6.5 then 6.6, and 6.7 before anything is shared

questions.question: How should you categorize the item you are reporting?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify the item type and category for the disputed transaction, offering examples like products or digital downloads to help you choose correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to ensure the disputed item is categorized accurately according to your specific purchase.
questions.check: Does the form ask for an item type or category, with examples like products or digital downloads?
questions.say_example: Categorized the item as <a physical product>

questions.question: How do you describe the specific item you are disputing?
questions.why: The form requires specific details like the item name, type, category, and quantity to accurately process the report for the problematic item.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose control over exactly how the disputed item is described and categorized, which could affect the outcome of your claim.
questions.check: Does the form ask for the item's name, type, category, and quantity?
questions.say_example: Entered the item name, type, and quantity

questions.question: How many items are you reporting in this dispute?
questions.why: Entering the exact quantity ensures the dispute claim accurately reflects the number of missing or incorrect items from the transaction.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify exactly how many items were problematic, which could result in an incorrect claim amount.
questions.check: Does the form ask for the number of items being disputed?
questions.say_example: Entered a quantity of <1>

questions.question: Does the page warn that not every purchase is covered by the Buyer Protection Policy?
questions.why: The screen warns that not all items are covered and advises checking the User Agreement to confirm eligibility.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to verify if their specific purchase is actually eligible for buyer protection before filing the dispute.
questions.check: Does the page warn that not all purchases are covered by the Buyer Protection Policy?
questions.say_example: This page warns not everything is covered by buyer protection. Worth checking this purchase type qualifies before going further.

questions.question: Do you need to add any additional items to this dispute?
questions.why: The screen displays the current item details alongside an 'Add another item' link, letting you include multiple items in a single claim if needed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to ensure all relevant items from the transaction are accurately included in the dispute before proceeding.
questions.check: Does the page show an 'Add another item' link alongside the current item's details?
questions.say_example: Added no additional items to this dispute

questions.question: Are the item details correct before you continue?
questions.why: The screen displays the details of the reported item and offers a link to add another item to the dispute.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify the item details and ensure all disputed items are included in the claim.
questions.check: Do the item details shown (name, category, quantity) match what's actually being disputed?
questions.say_example: The item listed here is <a blue jacket, qty 1>, matching what you said was missing.

questions.question: Is there a blank item row blocking the dispute form from submitting?
questions.why: Clicking 'Add another item' creates a mandatory set of blank fields, which will trigger a validation error and block submission unless you click the trash can to remove the empty row.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might get stuck on a form validation error, unable to submit the claim because they don't realize an empty, accidentally-added item row needs to be deleted.
questions.check: Does the form show a blank, unfilled item row alongside the one you meant to submit?
questions.say_example: There's an empty item row sitting here from 'Add another item'. It'll block submitting until it's removed.

questions.question: What total amount do you expect to be refunded, including any extra charges?
questions.why: The screen asks for the expected refund amount and explicitly notes to include miscellaneous charges like shipping or tax.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to ensure they are fully reimbursed for all associated costs of the disputed transaction.
questions.verify_form: A total refund amount went in - check it includes the shipping and tax you actually paid; the claim caps at what was typed.
questions.check: Does the form ask for a total refund amount, noting that it should include extra charges like shipping or tax?
questions.say_example: What's the full amount to claim, including shipping and tax? Only what's typed here gets refunded.

questions.question: When was the item delivered to you?
questions.why: The dispute form asks for the specific date the item was delivered to help investigate the claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to provide the exact delivery date from your personal records, which could affect the outcome of the dispute.
questions.check: Does the form ask for the date the item was delivered?
questions.say_example: Entered <15 March> as the delivery date

questions.question: What is the correct amount you should have been charged instead of what actually posted?
questions.why: The screen asks for the amount on your receipt or the amount you think you were charged to determine the exact amount being disputed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to specify the exact amount they believe they should have been charged, which could result in an incorrect refund.
questions.check: Does the receipt or stated correct amount differ from the amount actually charged?
questions.say_example: Your receipt says <$6.50>, the charge posted at <$8.05>. That's the gap this dispute is about.

questions.question: Is the dispute amount pre-filled with the full charge, even though you're only disputing part of it?
questions.why: The form often auto-populates the full charge amount by default, which must be manually overwritten if you are only disputing part of the transaction.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to catch a visually pre-filled value that might claim the wrong amount, potentially causing the bank to reject the dispute for inaccuracy.
questions.check: Does the dispute-amount field show the full transaction total pre-filled, when only part of the charge is being disputed?
questions.say_example: This field pre-filled the full <$48.20> charge. Since you're only disputing part of it, that needs changing before you submit.

questions.question: Did you already contact the seller about this charge, and if so, when and how?
questions.why: The dispute flow asks for details about any previous communication with the seller, including the date and method of contact, to understand if you tried to resolve it directly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might incorrectly report whether or how you tried to resolve the issue with the merchant directly, which could weaken your claim.
questions.check: Does the form ask whether and how you already contacted the seller?
questions.say_example: Noted contact with the seller on <10 March>, by email

questions.question: Do you need to retrieve timestamps or screenshots from external social media messages to prove you contacted the seller?
questions.why: The dispute process often requires proof of contact, meaning you may need to open external platforms like Twitter to retrieve the exact message history.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally locate and extract the exact external communication that proves you tried to resolve the issue with the merchant.
questions.verify_form: Proof of seller contact may live in your own external messages - check whether the agent needed it and what it pulled; those threads are yours to hand over or not.
questions.check: Does the dispute process ask for proof of contacting the seller, such as a screenshot from another platform?
questions.say_example: This step wants proof you messaged the seller. That may mean pulling a screenshot from <Twitter> or wherever you actually messaged them.

questions.question: What additional information do you want to provide to explain the issue?
questions.why: The screen provides a text box to explain the problem in your own words while warning against including confidential information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to articulate the specific context and nuances of why you are requesting a refund.
questions.verify_form: Free-text got written into the case - check what it says; those words are the version of events the reviewer reads.
questions.check: Does the form show a free-text box for explaining the issue, with a warning against including confidential information?
questions.say_example: The explanation says <item never arrived, ordered 1 March, no tracking updates since>. That's the version of events the reviewer will read.

questions.question: Do the amount, dates, and description you're about to submit match what actually happened with this charge?
questions.why: The form requires specific information like the amount, dates, and a description of the issue to advance the claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to ensure their specific situation is accurately represented to the bank.
questions.check: Do the amount, dates, and description entered so far match what actually happened with this charge?
questions.say_example: The description here says <item never arrived>, but the amount field still shows the full <$48.20> charge. Worth checking those line up before moving on.

questions.question: What supporting documents should you upload to support your case?
questions.why: The screen allows uploading supporting files but warns that these documents will be shared with the seller, meaning you must carefully exclude confidential information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over selecting which specific evidence to share with the seller while ensuring your sensitive personal information remains protected.
questions.verify_form: Files were chosen to support the case - check which ones, knowing everything uploaded is shown to the seller; the wrong screenshot hands them your private details.
questions.check: Does the page warn that uploaded documents will be shared directly with the seller?
questions.say_example: Whatever gets uploaded here goes straight to the seller. Worth checking it doesn't show anything private.

questions.question: Should you upload supporting documents or just provide a text explanation for the dispute?
questions.why: The screen offers an optional file upload area and a text box for additional details to help resolve the issue faster.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might skip uploading crucial evidence you possess or fail to articulate the specific nuances of your case, potentially weakening the dispute.
questions.verify_form: The agent decided between attaching documents and text alone - check whether the receipts you actually hold were uploaded; a text-only case is the weakest version of it.
questions.check: Does the page offer both a file-upload area and a text box as ways to support the claim?
questions.say_example: There's a choice here between uploading a document and just writing a description. The stronger evidence you actually have should go in, not just words.

questions.question: Did the file you selected actually appear in the attachments list?
questions.why: The interface might silently fail to attach a file if it exceeds the size limit or is the wrong format, so you must verify the file name is visible before submitting.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might submit the dispute without the crucial receipt or evidence if the upload silently failed and they didn't verify the attachment list.
questions.check: Does the attachments list show the file name after it was selected?
questions.say_example: The attachments list is still empty after choosing a file. It may not have actually attached.

questions.question: Does the file's thumbnail show a legible, correct document?
questions.why: The platform displays a small visual preview of the uploaded file, which is the only way to confirm the correct image was attached before submitting.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually verify that the attached file is the right receipt and is legible, which could cause the dispute to be rejected if the agent uploaded the wrong image.
questions.check: Does the uploaded file's thumbnail preview show a legible, correct document?
questions.say_example: The thumbnail here shows <a blurry photo>. Worth checking that's actually the receipt before submitting.

questions.question: Are your supporting documents in an acceptable file format and under the size limit?
questions.why: The upload tool strictly accepts specific formats (like JPG, PNG, or PDF) and enforces a maximum file size (e.g., 10MB), meaning unsupported or overly large files will fail to attach.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure your crucial evidence is actually accepted by the system, as an agent might silently fail to upload oversized photos or unsupported document types.
questions.check: Does the page state accepted file formats and a size limit for uploads?
questions.say_example: This upload area only takes files under <10MB> in <JPG, PNG or PDF>. Worth checking the file fits before relying on it.

questions.question: Does the page warn that this explanation will be shared with the seller?
questions.why: The screen displays a warning that any information included in the dispute form will be shared directly with the seller.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally screen the dispute explanation to ensure no sensitive or private details are exposed to the merchant.
questions.check: Does the page warn that the explanation will be shared directly with the seller?
questions.say_example: Whatever's written here goes straight to the seller. Worth a check that nothing private is in it.

children.label: Submit the claim
children.note: 7.1, 7.2 where the form demands declarations, 7.3 before anything files; then 7.4 - or 7.5 where the app routes completion to a phone line

questions.question: Are the dispute details and attached file accurate and ready to submit?
questions.why: Reviewing the explanation about the unreceived order and the attached image ensures the bank has the correct evidence to process the claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify that the agent accurately described the missing order and attached the correct supporting evidence before finalizing the dispute.
questions.check: Does the review page show the dispute details and attached file together as a summary before a submit control?
questions.say_example: Here's what's about to go in: <item not received>, <$48.20>, one attachment. Ready to submit, or want to change something first?

questions.question: Do you want to receive your claim documents and communications online or by regular mail?
questions.why: The platform asks if you want to switch to paperless delivery for faster and more secure access to your claim documents.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to control your account's document delivery preferences, which could result in missing important physical mail or unexpected changes to your settings.
questions.verify_form: A paperless-or-mail choice got made for your claim documents - check which; it silently rewrites how every future notice reaches you.
questions.check: Does the page offer a choice between paperless (online) and mail delivery for claim documents?
questions.say_example: This sets whether future claim notices come by email or regular mail. I set it to <online> unless you want mail.

questions.question: Are you signing a fraud affidavit under penalty of perjury by clicking submit?
questions.why: Formal fraud disputes often require you to legally attest that you did not authorize or benefit from the charge, and false claims can lead to account closure or legal consequences.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to read the legal disclosures and ensure you are comfortable taking legal responsibility for the fraud claim before the agent submits it on your behalf.
questions.verify_form: Submitting a fraud claim can be a sworn statement - check what the submission attested under your name; a false affidavit is your legal exposure, not the agent's.
questions.check: Does the page state that submitting attests, under penalty of perjury, that the charge was not authorized?
questions.say_example: Submitting this is a sworn statement that you didn't authorize the charge. A false one is real legal exposure to you, not me. Still want to submit?

questions.question: Does the page offer a provisional credit option while the dispute is investigated?
questions.why: Many institutions offer a temporary credit for the disputed amount, but they may require you to explicitly check a box or request it during the submission process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If the agent skips or misses the provisional credit option, you will be out of pocket for the disputed amount for the entire duration of the investigation, which can take up to 90 days.
questions.verify_form: A provisional credit may have needed an explicit opt-in - check whether the agent requested it; without it you are out the money for the whole investigation.
questions.check: Does the page offer an option to request a provisional credit while the dispute is investigated?
questions.say_example: There's a box here for a provisional credit while this gets investigated. I checked it, since without it you're out the money until it's resolved.

questions.question: Do you agree to the bank's declaration that the details you provided are accurate?
questions.why: The Chase dispute form requires you to explicitly check a box stating "I understand accurate and specific details help resolve my dispute faster" before allowing you to submit the claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally attest to the accuracy of your claim, which acts as a formal declaration to your bank.
questions.verify_form: The form required declaring your details accurate - check what got attested; that checkbox is your signature on the claim.
questions.check: Does the page require checking a box declaring the details provided are accurate before submitting?
questions.say_example: This checkbox is you declaring everything entered is accurate. That's your signature on the claim. Confirm to submit?

questions.question: Are you sure you want to report this transaction as a scam?
questions.why: Clicking 'Next' with 'I was scammed' selected will initiate a fraud investigation that could flag or close the recipient's account.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to halt the dispute process for a legitimate transaction, which could unjustly penalize the recipient.
questions.verify_form: The scam report sat one tap from filing - check it was not submitted casually; filing flags a real person's account, and this sender may be someone you know.
questions.check: Does the page show a final confirmation before filing a scam report with 'I was scammed' selected?
questions.say_example: This will file a scam report on <the recipient's> account and can get it flagged or closed. Sure you want to go ahead?

questions.question: What must you do to officially complete the claim?
questions.why: The screen explicitly states that a phone call to the provided number is required to finish the process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user would be unaware that the online process is incomplete and that they must make a phone call to finalize the dispute.
questions.check: Does the page state that a phone call to a given number is required to finish the process?
questions.say_example: This isn't finished yet. The page says you still need to call <the number shown> to complete the claim.

children.label: Track and manage the case
children.note: 8.1 the moment anything submits; 8.2 then 8.3 while the case sits open; 8.4 to 8.8 are the moves the case's state offers - escalate, retype, appeal through 8.6's own form, close, or re-report; 8.6's evidence and submission reuse 6.5, 6.6 and 7.1

questions.question: Is the dispute actually listed in your open cases?
questions.why: Although the submission seemed complete, the Resolution Center shows zero open cases, indicating the claim may not have been successfully recorded.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If the agent assumes the dispute was filed without verifying the open cases list, you might lose your money because the claim was never actually processed.
questions.check: Does the open-cases list or count reflect the dispute that was just submitted?
questions.say_example: The open-cases list still doesn't show this dispute after submitting. Worth checking it actually went through.

questions.question: How do you want to proceed now that the message to the seller has been sent?
questions.why: The screen confirms the message was sent to Wish.com and notes that PayPal can help if the issue isn't resolved directly, prompting a choice on what to do next.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to wait for the seller's response or immediately review the transaction details.
questions.verify_form: The message to the seller went out and the agent chose what to do next - check whether it is waiting for the reply or already escalating; the 20-day window is yours to spend.
questions.check: Does the page confirm a message was sent to the seller and mention a window to wait before PayPal can help?
questions.say_example: Your message to <the seller> went out. There's a window before you can bring PayPal in, so this is a choice of wait or escalate now.

questions.question: Is there an escalation deadline shown on the confirmation screen?
questions.why: The confirmation screen displays a green checkmark and a specific deadline to escalate the claim under the Purchase Protection Policy if the merchant does not resolve the issue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss seeing the confirmation checkmark and directly knowing the exact deadline to escalate the claim if the merchant fails to resolve it.
questions.check: Does the confirmation screen show a deadline to escalate the claim under a purchase-protection policy?
questions.say_example: There's an escalation deadline on this confirmation, <30 March>. Worth having that written down.

questions.question: What are the next steps and details of your submitted dispute?
questions.why: The screen confirms the dispute was successfully submitted and outlines next steps, such as accessing the claim in the Message Center.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the immediate reassurance of the successful submission and the specific instructions on how to track the claim's progress.
questions.check: Does the confirmation screen list next steps and where to find the claim (e.g. Message Center)?
questions.say_example: Submitted. Next steps: check <the Message Center> for updates, and the seller has a window to respond.

questions.question: Is there a claim or case reference number shown on the confirmation screen?
questions.why: The confirmation screen often displays a unique case or reference number that is required for future phone support, and it may not always be sent via email or appear immediately in the app's dispute history.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the only immediate record of the claim number if the agent navigates away from the transient success screen before writing it down.
questions.check: Does the confirmation screen show a case or reference number?
questions.say_example: Your claim reference is <PP-1029384>. That's shown here once, so worth writing down before leaving this screen.

questions.question: Which closed dispute case do you want to review?
questions.why: The screen lists multiple closed cases with different Case IDs and amounts, so you must select the correct one to view its specific details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify the history and resolution details of a specific past dispute.
questions.verify_form: The agent opened one of your closed cases - check it is the case you wanted revisited; each carries its own ID, amount and outcome.
questions.check: Does the page list multiple closed cases with different case IDs and amounts?
questions.say_example: Opened the closed case for <$48.20>

questions.question: Are any of your open disputes approaching the auto-close deadline shown on the dashboard?
questions.why: The dashboard flags 'Contestazioni da rivedere' as requiring your action, which is critical since unresolved disputes automatically close after 20 days.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate awareness of urgent deadlines and the context of which specific disputes are at risk of being automatically closed.
questions.check: Does the dashboard flag a dispute as needing review, with a day-count before it auto-closes?
questions.say_example: One of your disputes is flagged as needing review. It auto-closes in <12 days> if nothing's done.

questions.question: Which open dispute do you want to review or escalate?
questions.why: The Resolution Center displays multiple open cases, requiring you to identify the correct case number, such as [number], to view its details or convert it into a claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over the timing of the escalation, as an agent might convert the dispute to a claim before you feel the seller has had adequate time to respond.
questions.verify_form: The agent selected an open case to act on - check which case, and whether it escalated anything; converting a dispute to a claim ends the seller conversation on a clock you may have wanted to run longer.
questions.check: Does the Resolution Center list more than one open case?
questions.say_example: Opened case <#12345> from the open-cases list

questions.question: Are these the correct details for the dispute case you are reviewing?
questions.why: Expanding the case details allows you to verify the disputed amount, seller information, and shipping address to ensure the correct claim is being handled.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally verify that the correct transaction and seller details were accurately recorded for your dispute.
questions.check: Do the expanded case details (amount, seller, shipping address) match what you expect for this dispute?
questions.say_example: This case shows <$48.20> to <Riverside Coffee>, shipped to <123 Main St>. That matches what you filed.

questions.question: What is the outcome and timeline of your dispute?
questions.why: Reviewing the case timeline confirms that the dispute was closed in your favor and a refund was issued.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss the direct reassurance of seeing the exact resolution timeline and the confirmation of your refund.
questions.check: Does the case timeline show a final outcome (e.g. closed in your favor) and whether a refund was issued or only provisional?
questions.say_example: This case closed in your favor. <$48.20> refunded. That's final, not a provisional hold.

questions.question: How do you know who is reviewing the dispute after the seller responds?
questions.why: The dashboard updates to show 'In corso di revisione da parte di PayPal', indicating that PayPal has taken over the review process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the reassurance of seeing exactly where their dispute stands and who is currently responsible for the next step.
questions.check: Does the dashboard show who is currently reviewing the dispute (e.g. 'under review by PayPal')?
questions.say_example: Status shows <under review by PayPal> now that the seller has responded

questions.question: Do you want to send a message to the seller or mark the issue as resolved?
questions.why: The screen displays an open case for a $6.00 payment to KeepCalling with options to either message the seller or close the dispute, which determines the next step in the resolution process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to communicate further with the seller or close the case based on their own assessment of the situation.
questions.verify_form: The open case offered message-the-seller or mark-resolved - check which the agent took; resolved closes the door on the refund.
questions.check: Does the open case show options to message the seller or mark the issue as resolved?
questions.say_example: This case is open for <$6.00> to <KeepCalling>. Marking it resolved closes the door on getting that back. Message them instead, or really resolved?

questions.question: How do you escalate the unresolved dispute to PayPal?
questions.why: The screen displays a warning that the case will automatically close by a specific date unless you click 'Inoltra a PayPal' to convert it into a formal claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over the timing of the escalation, as you might prefer to wait for the merchant's response before officially involving PayPal.
questions.verify_form: The agent may have escalated the dispute to a formal claim - check whether it did and when; escalation ends the seller conversation for good, and you may have wanted to wait out a reply.
questions.check: Does the page show an option to escalate the unresolved dispute to a formal claim (e.g. 'Inoltra a PayPal'), with a warning that the case will otherwise auto-close by a date?
questions.say_example: This case auto-closes on <20 March> unless escalated. Escalating ends the conversation with the seller for good. Ready to escalate now, or wait for their reply?

questions.question: Should you change the case type to better fit the issue you are facing?
questions.why: The screen offers alternative options like reporting a lost card or an unauthorized subscription to ensure the dispute is categorized correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify if a different dispute category better matches the specific details of your fraudulent transaction.
questions.verify_form: The agent may have changed the case type - check what the case now claims; item-not-received and not-as-described are judged by different rules, and the switch is usually one-way.
questions.check: Does the page offer alternative case types (e.g. lost card, unauthorized subscription) for an already-filed case?
questions.say_example: This case is filed as <item not received>. Switching it to <unauthorized subscription> is usually one-way and judged by different rules. Still want to change it?

children.label: Appeal the outcome
children.note: 8.6.1 then 8.6.2; the evidence and the submission reuse 6.5, 6.6 and 7.1

questions.question: What are the details of the case you need to appeal?
questions.why: The email displays the specific case ID and outcome needed to identify which transaction to address in PayPal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to review the specific context and case number of the dispute before taking action in your account.
questions.check: Does the email or page show the case ID and outcome for the case being appealed?
questions.say_example: Appealed case <#98765>, closed as <denied>

questions.question: What is your reason for filing this appeal?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify whether you will provide tracking information or proof of a previous refund to support your appeal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might select an appeal reason you cannot actually provide proof for, which could cause your claim to be denied.
questions.verify_form: An appeal reason got selected - check it is one you can actually prove; an appeal filed on evidence you do not hold is denied on arrival.
questions.check: Does the appeal form ask for a reason, such as providing tracking information or proof of a prior refund?
